posts.content_md:
It's a simple question, and I hope the answer is equally simple.

When bleaching my H1 transmission masters with ferric EDTA following development in CW-C2, I always wash away the bleach and start with new bleach for my next H1

Conversely, when making an H2 white light viewable image plane final hologram using Saxby's pyrochrome process followed by an acid dichromate bleach - I always pour the bleach back into the stock bottle to use again ..... and it works fine time after time

Is there any sound reason for such action - can I use the ferric EDTA bleach repeatedly until the bleaching process slows down, as I will do with the acid dichromate bleach

The film I use is red sensitive AGFA, which although now old, works just fine and a 30 mW HeNe

John

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: You can store and re-use both the the ferric EDTA bleach and the dichromate bleaches. They both work in the same way anyhow since they're both reverible bleaches. You may want to keep the bleach in one of those containers that Jeff mentions that can be collapsed to expel all the air so that no oxygen or CO2 gets into the bleach.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** You can store and re-use both the the ferric EDTA bleach and the dichromate bleaches.

Yes, I've got a ferric EDTA bleach I've been using for almost 20 years (and it's still working).

> You may want to keep the bleach in one of those containers that Jeff mentions that can be collapsed to expel all the air so that no oxygen or CO2 gets into the bleach.

Ferric EDTA bleach does actually require oxygen to regenerate (converting ferrous into ferric EDTA again).

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
> They both work in the same way anyhow since they're both reverible bleaches

The Pyrochrome is a reversal bleach, which is what I think you are trying to say, while the Fe EDTA is a rehalogenating bleach.

Eventually the Pyrochrome dichromate reversal bleaches (and there are dichromate based rehalogenating bleaches, the Kodak R-10 series for example) get so loaded with dissolved silver compounds that they can't hold any more. Dropping some table salt in them will precipitate some nice chunks of silver chloride. Store in the dark or you can watch them print out in the light! And maybe you can still keep using the bleach!

The Ferric EDTA bleaches like exposure to air! It regenerates the oxidizer. What kills these bleaches is too much alkali developer getting carried over from not washing well between them. Maybe some more acid to lower the pH might help if the bleach slows down. And I doubt if all of the Br ions would get used up with the relatively small amount of material that gets put through the solutions in a typical holo lab. I've got some made up that is a few years old.

The organic oxidizer based rehalogenating bleaches do go bad after a day or so, like the beloved PBQ and the PBU series, although with the latter the persulfate will keep regenerating the oxidizer for longer life.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **Ed Wesly:** The Pyrochrome is a reversal bleach, which is what I think you are trying to say

Yes, I meant reversal. I use the term reversible.

> **Ed Wesly:** while the Fe EDTA is a rehalogenating bleach.

Yes, that's true. I never used a Fe EDTA bleach so I always assumed it was a reversible bleach. I just looked it up and it is a rehal bleach. I use PBU, which I put in a fridge (a separate fridge in the lab just for chemicals!) I generally make up a litre of the stuff, use it 200 mls at a time, and throw it out at the end of the day. At the next shoot, I replenish from the fridge. Once or twice I've had to develop very large plates for which I've had to use 2 litres of bleach and developed just two or three plates. I kept the used bleach since it seemed a little wasteful to develop just three plates and then throw out the entire two 2 litres.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: Ferric sulphate based bleaches get stinky (sulfuric) with age. I throw them out at that point, even though they seem to still work OK. Given the low cost relative to film/plates etc it seems not too wasteful, but I wonder when they really do stop working...

posts.author: John Sonley
posts.content_md:
Gentlemen - thank you so much for all your replies and in future I will not be so wasteful in washing away my ferric/EDTA bleach each time I use it.

Noted also that contaminants from the developing process will degrade the bleach - but I always wash well with clean water between CW-C2 development and the ferric/EDTA bleach

Just adding to this story, I find that CW-C2 Solution A only has a lifetime of about 2 months, even when stored in a fridge. If you keep and use it for longer than that, it starts to slow down and processing takes longer.

I've just made a new batch - 500mls only - which lasts me for a month or so - it was slightly faster than my 2 month old batch - - not orders of magnitude, but visibly faster.

CW-C2 Solution B lasts for ever ---------- however long ever is!

BRgds

John

Yes, I think rinsing before bleaching also helps reduce image noise. I do a final soak in distilled water to get rid of any stray chlorine/minerals which could cause cloudy precipitates in the emulsion.

Re: Part A lifetime, for the JD-4 metol/ascorbic acid devoloper I find that Part A lasts many months when refrigerated. Eventually it turns orange/brown, but still seems to work OK. Given the cost of time and materials for holograms versus the risk of bad results from old chemistry, I just flush it at that time. "If it's yellow, let it mellow - if it's brown, flush it down"

posts.author: holorefugee
posts.content_md: All rinses and raw water for mixing chemistry should be chlorine and chloride free. This is really important!
